The two measurement-dependent rows flip only at the extreme multiplier -- which is exactly what their verdict means. The face was right and the assertion was wrong (r1281's assertion-vs-flag shape), so the leg now pins the published flag pair (`flips_on_any_measurement` / `flips_on_every_measurement`) instead of one draw. Second pit: `_write` called `io.dump` instead of `json.dump`, so every function-level selftest was green while `run()` died on first save -- run and selftest are a pair (r1281 pit 1, second occurrence).

How to apply: > when a band is a finite-sample quantile, a published "outside" verdict must be re-read at the widest grid the ladder supports before it is called a finding -- publish how many survive, not just that the band moved; > a multiplier derived on one window is NOT that window's multiplier for another window: publish the whole (family x rung) product as a range and call a row "flipped" only when it flips at every one; > a row count over-states the finding when two faces publish the same number -- publish the distinct-coefficient count beside it; > before re-judging a row, reproduce its published flag from its own numbers, otherwise you are silently replacing a published verdict with your own arithmetic.

### E258 -- a draw-count multiplier is a property of the window it was measured in (r1285 bm-b)

`scripts/e258_band_multiplier_per_window.py` (selftest 21/21) -- face `results/state_tilt/BANDWINMULT-2026-10-29.json`

E257 had to BORROW the draw multiplier: the ladder was measured only inside `era_2025_now` and the resulting range applied to every published window, because a fixed window is neither that era's head nor its tail. E258 measures instead: it rebuilds the paired shuffled band INSIDE each published window, pinning the window's own dates, the star that cell published AND the cell's own member list, then publishes `m = edge(1920 draws)/edge(published draws)` with its per-seed scatter.

Reading (4 windows measured; 2 skipped because they publish no star at lag 0). At each window's own published base count: all_five 1.317 (base 200), early_three 1.838 (base 60), era_2023_2024 1.473 (base 60), era_2025_now 1.644 (base 60) -- spread 1.267..1.838 over the eight window/base cells, ratio 1.45. Re-judging the 16 published rows with each row's own window multiplier: 8 survive outside, 2 stay inside, 2 flip only for some seeds (one coefficient, b = -0.4942, published twice), 4 unjudgeable.

What the measurement actually buys: **resolution, not correction**. Same-base comparison (each row's measured multiplier vs the range E257 applied to that row at the same draw count) is 0 of 12 rows outside. But the median borrowed range was **0.820 wide** while the median per-window seed width is **0.256** -- a 3.2x narrower judgement, because the borrowed range spanned ladder rung lengths the row never had.

Pits this round: ① the first cut measured every window on the five-member basket; `early_three` is a THREE-member window, so intersecting five level series over 2013-2016 returned 0 sessions and the face read as "unmeasurable" when the cause was the wrong universe -- pin dates + star + MEMBERS. ② `published_verdicts()` returned only the verdict string and a later `rec.update(...)` overwrote the attached value with `None`, so the comparison column printed `n/a..n/a` for all sixteen rows (worse than absent: it reads as "E257 has no range"). ③ the first narrative claimed early_three was "under-widened by 10.5%", which compared a 60-draw measurement against a 200-draw table range; re-read at the same base it was inside its own range. The cross-base block is still published with a `BASIS_WARNING`, and the same-base block is the headline. ④ the seeded card declared `..._per_window.py` / `BANDWINMULT-<cutoff>.json`; writing `..._in_each_window.py` / `WINDOWMULT-*` would have left a phantom card (`runner_absent`) -- names come from the card.

How to apply: > when a face borrows a parameter measured elsewhere, treat the borrow as a named compromise and measure it where it is applied as soon as a build exists; > anything pinned from a published cell must pin the whole universe (dates + star + MEMBERS) -- a star pinned into a wider basket is a different experiment whose failure looks like "no data"; > before comparing a multiplier (or any scaled quantity) to a published range, check that both sides were read at the SAME base -- two bases, one subtraction is not a comparison; > a borrowed range that spans rungs the row never had is wide for a reason that has nothing to do with the row: publish the width beside the point and let the reader see the resolution gain; > a multiplier from 3 seeds is a range -- say `depends_on_seed_scatter` rather than picking the median.


### E259 -- a multiplier published as min..max over three seeds is a range, not a distribution (r1286 bm-b)

`scripts/e259_band_multiplier_distribution.py` (selftest 30/30) -- face `results/state_tilt/BANDWINDIST-2026-10-29.json`

E258 published each window's draw multiplier as `min..max` over **three** shuffle streams, and every
"outside at every seed" statement in the star family rested on that range. Three draws are not a
distribution. E259 rebuilds the same band inside the same four published windows with **40**
independent prefix-nested streams (the first three are E258's exact seeds) and publishes the
sample's own `[p05, p95]` per (window, leg, published base count), then re-judges every published
row at the interval's tight end, its median, and its wide end.

Reading: 16 of 16 intervals are **wider** than the three-seed range they replace -- ratios 1.09..
**11.77**, median **2.25**. Width 0.519..1.196 (median 0.827). Of 16 re-judged rows, 10 are outside
at the median, 2 inside, 4 unjudgeable; **3 change verdict inside their own interval** (outside at
the tight end and at the median, inside at the wide end -- `early_three` cross and `early_three`
star lag-1 residual, both `b = -0.4942`, plus `era_2023_2024`'s residual at `b = -0.8332`); 7 are
outside at every end. The worst understatement is `era_2025_now self:60`: three seeds said the range
was 0.088 wide, forty streams say 1.040 (11.77x). E258's own three-seed per-seed table reproduces
bit-for-bit on 8/8 of the arms it published.

Degenerate reading, published rather than cleaned: **52 of 640** per-seed multipliers are *exactly*
1.0, because a prefix-nested band's endpoint cannot move again once the draw that sets it has
already arrived inside the base prefix. Those seeds drag `p05` to 1.000 in 14 of 16 arms; dropping
them as degenerate would make the interval narrower and prettier than the streams it came from.

Pit this round: **a lookup keyed more coarsely than the arm it claims to read silently returns
another arm's numbers.** E258's window record is keyed by base count alone and carries the default
leg, so it holds the SELF stream; this face's first run looked up `cross:60`, read the self stream,
and reported `8/16` "non-reproducing" rows -- a pure lookup error dressed as a non-reproduction.
The pin now covers only the arm E258 published (8/8) and the other eight say
`e258_published = no`. Sibling: `run` and `verify` are a pair -- `verify` re-derives each interval
from the stored per-seed streams and each row's median verdict from its own arm's multiplier.

How to apply: > never publish a Monte-Carlo parameter as `min..max` over a handful of seeds --
publish the sample's quantiles and the seed count so the reader sees the resolution; > when a face
stores a table under a coarser key than the arm it belongs to, every downstream lookup must carry
the arm name or it will read the wrong stream and blame the upstream face; > count and publish the
degenerate streams that a prefix-nest admits (multiplier exactly 1.0) instead of letting them set
the interval's floor invisibly; > a verdict that only holds at one end of a published interval is
`interval_dependent`, not flipped.

## E260 -- the published base draw count sits below the endpoint arrival count

A Monte-Carlo band's draw count can be *below settlement*, and that is measurable rather than a
worry. Because E259's streams are prefix-nested, each seed's band endpoint is non-decreasing in the
draw count, so for every seed there is a first count at which it stops moving: its ARRIVAL. Read
back at every grid point, arrival becomes a distribution per window, and the question "is the
published band a converged band?" becomes an arithmetic comparison instead of an opinion.

Measured on the E252/E257/E258/E259 band family (4 windows x 2 legs x 40 seeds, no new draws):
median arrival **1440 draws** against published base counts of **60 / 200**; **174 of 320** seeds
reach their final endpoint only at the top of the grid; **12 of 16** published rows sit below their
own arrival count and **0 of 16** settle at their base. A multiplier of exactly 1.0 is the
degenerate reading of the same object: the endpoint already arrived before the base count, which is
why E259 counted 52 of 640 -- this face reproduces that count arm by arm (16/16, 52/52).

How to apply: > before reading a Monte-Carlo band as converged, publish the arrival distribution of
the draw count and compare it with the count actually used -- "the endpoint is still rising" is a
statement about a knob, "the median seed needs 1440 draws and the band is published at 200" is a
statement a reader can act on; > a prefix-nested sample makes arrival *well defined*, which is the
reason to nest rather than to redraw independently at each count; > when the arrival floor sits at
the top of the grid, the grid is the binding constraint -- publish that instead of implying the
sample converged; > pin a cross-face reproduction ARM BY ARM (key = base count *and* leg), never by
summing whatever rows happen to be published: the published rows and the distribution arms were two
different 16s, and the 29-vs-52 "reproduction failure" was that mistake, not a broken upstream.

## E261 -- the floor at one belongs to the attained bucket, not to the stream

A Monte-Carlo band built on prefix-nested draws has a *degenerate* reading: once the draw that sets a
band endpoint has already arrived inside the base prefix, that endpoint cannot move again and the
seed's multiplier is exactly one. E259 published 52 of 640 such seeds. The question a reader needs is
what those seeds cost: if you take the bucket out, does the interval move a little (the floor was the
stream's own bound) or a lot (the floor was arrival)?

Measured by rebuilding every published interval twice on the same per-seed table (E259's face only,
no new draws): **8 of 16 arms carry a floor at one and all 8 leave it** when the bucket is removed --
median lift **+0.0734** (range +0.0327..+0.2005), median width loss **10.4%** of itself (max 18.2%).
The floor is **not spread evenly across base counts**: **7 of 8 at base 200, 1 of 8 at base 60**,
which is the direction E260's arrival result predicts. The bucket sits at the bottom of the
distribution, so removing it moves the median by only +0.0148. **No published row verdict depends on
the bucket** (0 of 16 rows re-judged).

How to apply: > before quoting "this band can only widen", publish the interval with and without the
endpoint-attained bucket -- a floor that moves was arrival, not a bound; > a trimmed sample selects on
its own minimum, so it answers "how far can it still move", never "where does it land", and it makes
"outside" easier -- publish that direction so a newly-outside row cannot be read as a finding; > a
floor that concentrates in one base count is a statement about arrival, so publish the cross-tab
rather than leaving it for the reader to compute; > a lookup keyed by (window, base count) alone
silently returns the wrong leg -- E259's row table re-judged the cross and lag-1 rows against the self
arm; this face resolves leg-less rows by the coefficient they publish and names the ambiguity (1 of 16
verdicts moves when fixed, in the easier direction).

### E263 -- a draw budget is neither a length effect nor a band effect, and a censored column is not a response (r1289 bm-b)

E260 measured where each window's band endpoint stops moving and found the published base counts (60/200) far below the arrival (median 1440 draws). The obvious next question -- is the cost a property of the LENGTH of the window, or of the NARROWNESS of its band -- decides whether the fix is a per-window budget or one flat floor, and the answer is NEITHER: across 8 arms spanning 3.3x in sessions (440..1442) and 1.39x in the resolution ratio (spread / half the published band width), Spearman(settled area, sessions) = +0.000 (p=1.000) and Spearman(settled area, resolution ratio) = -0.167 (p=0.711); inside the arms the per-seed channel does not carry the band rival either (median rho +0.108, 5 of 8 arms POSITIVE where "a tighter claim needs more draws" predicts negative, sign test p=0.727). Read together with the published power floor (the smallest |rho| an 8-arm design can call at p<0.05 is 0.738, enumerated over all 40,320 orderings), the operative conclusion is that the draw requirement is roughly uniform across these windows -- so a per-window budget is a knob that buys nothing and the honest fix is one flat floor applied everywhere.

Three reusable pieces:

> the response must be the SETTLED-SHARE CURVE, not the arrival median -- the median is right-censored at the top of the grid (174 of 320 seeds arrive only AT 1920, so their true arrival is unknown), and a median over a censored column saturates at the ceiling in 5 of 8 arms and carries no rank information; the share settled at a fixed draw count is uncensored, monotone in arrival, and publishes the whole curve instead of one number.
> a null result needs its power printed on it -- enumerate the exact critical |rho| for the arm count you actually have (n<=8 is 40,320 orderings, cheap) rather than leaving the reader to decide whether "not significant" means "no effect" or "no design".
> when two rivals share a predicted SIGN, the discriminating quantity is WHICH covariate clears, not which way it points; publish both channels side by side and let the verdict name the channel that answered, or name that neither did.

Engineering pit caught in the same round, on this face's own first run: `(face.get("x") or {}.get("k"))` -- the `.get` binds to the `{}` literal, so a truthy left side returns the WHOLE block, and a field named `arms_recomputing_e260_arrival` published a dict where a count belonged. The summary printed it in plain sight; the fix carries a leg asserting `isinstance(..., int)`.

证据：scripts/e263_arrival_vs_cell_size.py（selftest 38/38 · verify 0 problems）、results/state_tilt/BANDARRIVALATE-2026-10-29.json（verdict=arrival_is_neither_channel · 8/8 arms 与 E260 arrivals 逐位复现）、source faces BANDARRIVAL/BANDWINDIST-2026-10-29。
## E262 -- another window's wide end is not a bound, and "use the widest" is invisible where it matters

E259 published a p05..p95 interval per (window, leg, base count) and closed with "the interval is not a three-seed range". The act it left untested is the one a reader performs: BORROW a wide end from another window and judge a row with it. Measured on E259's published intervals only (no draws, no panel, no refit): 16 arms, and the widest arm is not the same window at every group -- all_five at self:60 (2.1808) and cross:60 (2.2963), early_three at self:200 (1.7186), era_2025_now at cross:200 (1.7816), with spreads of 9.1%..16.8% to the narrowest arm in each group. So "use the widest" has no single referent.

What it costs when it is used anyway: 2 of 48 ordered (donor, recipient) pairs move a verdict, both from all_five's cross:60 wide end (+13.9% / +16.7% over the recipient's own) and both in the same direction -- outside -> inside, i.e. two rejections lost (era_2023_2024 star_lag1_residual b=-0.8332 and era_2025_now cross b=-0.9113). Nothing invents a rejection in this table. The pooled flat read -- one p95 per (leg, base), which is what "use the widest" actually adopts -- moves the same 2 rows at cross:60 and 0 at the other three groups: pooling is harmless everywhere except exactly where it matters, which is why the damage is invisible to inspection.

Three reusable pieces:

> a transfer must be published only inside one (leg, base count) -- the multiplier divides edge(top) by edge(base), so a 60-draw and a 200-draw arm of the same leg are different quantities, not two estimates of one (published as cross_base_offset: ratio median 1.35 self / 1.25 cross, and never mixed into the matrix).
> "not a bound" requires a MOVED ROW, not a wide spread -- a face with big interval differences and no moved verdict must say the wide end transfers without moving anything; the verdict function reads the rows, and a selftest leg pins that a big spread with no move does not produce the "not a bound" verdict.
> a residual carries no leg: resolve it by coefficient identity against that cell's own published rows, and publish unresolved/ambiguous rows rather than guessing -- E259's row table judged every row on the self arm, so resolving each row on its own leg moves exactly 1 wide-end verdict (era_2023_2024 star_lag1_residual: outside at every end on the cross arm, interval-dependent on the self arm). Disclosure list, not a rewrite of the upstream face.

Engineering pits caught in the same round: a fixture that already sits inside its own band cannot test a WIDENING (b=-0.5 against band +-0.3 scaled by 2 is inside both before and after; a direction leg needs a row just outside the own band, b=-0.7 vs +-0.6); `dominator()` returns None on a tie at the maximum by design, so the leg asserting a named winner on a tie was the wrong assertion, not the wrong code (r1281 shape); a two-cell group has 2 ordered pairs but only 1 donor per named recipient, and conflating the two fails three correct assertions; and PowerShell does not take heredocs (`python - <<'PY'`), so the patch round must go through a file or the edit tool (r1288 pit re-confirmed).

Evidence: scripts/e262_p95_transfer_across_windows.py (selftest 43/43, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDTRANSFER-2026-10-29.json (verdict=a_foreign_wide_end_is_not_a_bound; 48 pairs, 2 moved, 0 invented), source face BANDWINDIST-2026-10-29 (E259), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261030-r1290-e262-p95-transfer.md.


## E264 -- the floor at one is a bucket, not a row-side hazard, and every row that sits close sits close to the WIDE end

E259 published 40 independent multipliers per (window, leg, base count) and E261 showed the floor at exactly one belongs to the endpoint-already-attained bucket. Both are statements about the band. The row side is one number: a row's verdict at multiplier m is `outside <=> m < m*` with `m* = |b| / max(|lo|,|hi|)`, so m* -- not the interval -- decides where the row flips, and no draw is needed to compute it.

Measured on E259's published face only: 12 of 16 rows are readable (the 4 unread are pre2020_four and era_2020_2022, self and cross -- no coefficient or no band, disclosed not absorbed). 4 rows end exactly on the floor, and dropping every near-one seed lifts p05 to 1.110..1.201 (median shift 0.090, max 0.201) while moving ZERO tight-end verdicts: those four carry m* between 2.14 and 3.08, so the floor would have to roughly double to reach them. The floor is real, and nothing is standing on it.

Where rows DO sit close is the wide end: era_2025_now cross:60 has m*=1.9583 against its own p95=1.9678 -- a 0.0095 gap, 0.48% of the multiplier; then era_2023_2024 self:60 (0.0757) and era_2023_2024 star_lag1_residual cross:60 (0.1223). Median gap over the twelve is 0.413, max 1.551, so the distribution is lopsided rather than uniformly tight.

Three reusable pieces:

> when a band interval has a floor and you worry the floor is propping up rejections, ASK THE ROWS IN THEIR OWN UNITS -- m* = |b|/max(|lo|,|hi|) is the entire row-side story, it costs one division, and it turns a qualitative worry into a distance. Here the distance was >= 1.1 in every case, which is a much stronger statement than "the floor moved by 0.2".

> an interval end that is exactly a constant (p05 == 1.0) is a MEASUREMENT, not a margin -- its membership is a bucket (E261), so the counterfactual that matters is "drop the bucket and re-read", and the answer must be published as a verdict change count, not as a shift size. A 0.20 shift with zero verdict moves and a 0.02 shift with two are the same number of words and opposite findings.

> a "closest rows" ranking must disclose its tie rule and its top-k agreement with whatever independently moved rows -- here both rows E262 moved by borrowing sit inside the top-3 closest, and the third-closest did not move because no published donor reaches its m*=2.10, so the ranking is a SUPERSET of the damage rather than an equivalence. Publishing the superset/equivalence distinction is what keeps the ranking from being read as a screen it has not been tested as.

Engineering pits caught in the same round: the first fixture asserted "inside at the floor, outside without it" while the code returned outside -> inside -- at `outside <=> m < m*` dropping the floor RAISES m past m*, losing the rejection, so the assertion had the flip backwards (r1281 shape, the assertion was wrong); e262.row_records reads `band_draws` off the row while the fixture carried `base`, which fails on a missing key rather than a wrong number; and a near-one flag tested on existence would flag rows whose floor is nowhere near their threshold, so it is the conjunction of "tight end was the floor" AND "dropping it moves the verdict" (E207/E208 family).

Evidence: scripts/e264_near_one_seeds_reading.py (selftest 26/26, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDNEAR1-2026-10-29.json (verdict=closest_row_survives_without_them; 12/16 read, 4 on the floor, 0 dependent, closest gap 0.0095), source faces BANDWINDIST-2026-10-29 (E259) + BANDTRANSFER-2026-10-29 (E262), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261030-r1291-e264-near-one-rows.md.

## E266 -- a donor above the row is not yet a screen; the threshold is per SIDE

> "Any donor whose p95 exceeds the row's threshold flips that row" scores **2/18** on E262's published pairs (precision 0.111). The failure is not noise: **12** of the 16 false positives are rows the donor could never break (their own end had already rejected nothing -- the row sat inside its own band), and **4** are rows their own end does reject but the donor does not reach, because `max(|lo|,|hi|)` is the flip multiplier only on the **wider** side. A row below a band whose lower end is the narrow one crosses at `|b|/|lo|`, a LARGER number, so the published form understates how close it sits. **18 of 36** comparisons in the pool are of that shape -- half the readable pool, not a corner case.

> The corrected screen is a three-part conjunction, and dropping any part is measurable: threshold on the row's **own side** (`t_side`), the row must already be rejected by its own end (`own_p95 < t_side`), and the donor must cross that same threshold (`donor_p95 > t_side`). Guarding on the row's own end with the *max-end* threshold removes every false positive but then **loses a real move**: the one row whose own p95 sits above `t_max_end` and below `t_side` (era_2025_now cross, 1.9678 between 1.9583 and 2.1965) reads as "inside at its own end" while the borrowed donor does break it. An exact-on-the-fitted-arm screen that is wrong on the side it never looked at is the E213 family one axis over.

> Exactness at 2 positives over 36 comparisons is a **consistency check, not a validated screen** -- publish it that way, plus which direction class is empty (here `rejections_invented` = 0, so the screen's ability to predict flip DIRECTION is untested at this size). The cheapest honest expansion is a buffer/margin axis, not a bigger claim.

Engineering pits born here: (1) the counterexample list labelled all 16 false positives "its own end had already rejected this row" -- one explanation copied onto two mechanistically different classes (E207 family); the field now derives from `own_verdict`, not from prose. (2) `base` is not a stable key across these faces -- E262 rows carry `base`, E259-style source rows carry `band_draws` -- so reading only `base` produced **0 comparisons** on the fixture and an "exact" screen over nothing (r1261 both-curves-equal shape, one file over); `base_of()` now reads either key.

Evidence: scripts/e266_wide_end_screen_holdout.py (selftest 26/26, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDSCREEN-2026-10-29.json (verdict=donor_above_the_row_is_not_a_screen; 36 comparisons / 2 moves / S3 exact), source face BANDTRANSFER-2026-10-29 (E262), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261030-r1292-e266-wide-end-screen.md.

## E267 -- a margin is not a substitute for the row's own side

> E266's bracket screen is exact on 36 published comparisons and is a knife edge: a donor `0.0001` above the row's own-side threshold reads the same as one `0.3` above. Sweeping `donor_p95 > t*(1+b)` over four rules (own-side guard on/off x `t_side`/`t_max_end`) on the same comparisons answers whether a buffer can buy precision: **no**. The unbuffered side rule flags 14 of 36 with 2 moves (precision **0.143**); the best buffer over 43 exact breakpoints reaches **0.154** and only inside a b window **0.00116 wide** (0.04429..0.04545). The own-side guard alone is **2/2 exact at b=0** and stays exact for every b up to **0.0454** -- so a buffer is a free tightening on top of the guard and never an alternative to it.

> The binding fact is that separability is decided by the **largest** non-move, not the nearest: the nearest non-move clears its threshold by 0.0443 against the nearest move's 0.0455 (a 0.0012 gap that invites "a tiny buffer separates them"), but one non-move clears by **2.4595 (246%)**, so any b that clears every non-move (b=2.46) clears every move too. `separable=false`, `separating_b_window=null`, and both orderings published in full. Corollary for reading these faces: the six largest-clearance non-moves (1.24..2.46) are all `own:inside` rows -- donors at 2.5x the threshold that move nothing because there is no rejection to take away.

> Two ladders read differently and only one is safe to report: predictions, tp and fp are **non-increasing** in b (a buffer can only remove flags), while **precision is not monotone** -- it peaks at 0.154 and then falls to 0.0 when the last move dies at its own margin (`first_b_with_no_true_positive = 0.0739`). A curve that is read only at its peak therefore hides that the peak is a two-point coincidence; publish the whole ladder, `b >= 0` only (a buffer demands more clearance; accepting a donor below the threshold is another rule), and make the b grid the observed **breakpoints** so the curve is exact rather than sampled.

Engineering pits born here: (1) `summary["moves"]` was written twice in one dict literal -- count, then list -- so the list won, the count never shipped, and the new smoke leg's `isinstance(..., int)` assertion caught it as a bare `moves` key (E207 family, now rejected outright); use `moves_published` / `moves_detail` (E266 convention). (2) `separation()` first keyed `interleaved` on nearest-non-move vs the *furthest* move -- true for almost any population and would have claimed non-separability everywhere; the predicate must be largest-non-move vs nearest-move. Both selftest fixtures were miscast at first (both "separated" and "interleaved" were separable) and the legs caught them.

Evidence: scripts/e267_screen_buffer_margin.py (selftest 36/36, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDMARGIN-2026-10-29.json (verdict=buffer_cannot_buy_precision_itself; 36 comparisons / 2 moves / guarded_side exact at 12 b values), source face BANDSCREEN-2026-10-29 (E266), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261030-r1293-e267-buffer-margin.md.

## E268 -- the screen survives on the published table, but only through the tight pooled end, and only because nothing sits near the line

> E267 left the operative half of the wide-end screen resting on the row's own p95 -- the one number a reader who did not draw that row's band does not have. Two substitutes do live in the same published face: the (leg, base) group's pooled ends (`flat_p95`, `flat_tight_p95`) and the row's own published wide verdict (a boolean). Swapping only the own-end slot on the identical 36 comparisons / 2 moves: the **pooled tight end reproduces both moves with 0 false positives** and, more than that, **answers the guard identically on all 36 comparisons** (24 below t, 12 above; 0 disagreements), so it is a *disclosure*. The **pooled wide end** flips **6** comparisons and misses both moves, and the **published boolean** flips **3**.

> The per-row boolean is not the recomputed own-side verdict, and that is the interesting part: on `era_2023_2024 star_lag1_residual` (index 13) the boolean says **inside** while the row's own p95 (2.0161) sits below its cross-arm threshold (2.1384), i.e. outside. The boolean is E259's self-arm judgement, so a reader holding it inherits the arm E262 already disclosed as interval-dependent -- the substitution is not "same number, different source", it is **a different leg**. Publish it as a change of meaning, not a rounding error.

> Equivalence at 0 disagreements is only as strong as the distance to the line: the nearest comparison sits **0.0835** off its threshold (4.43%, index 15) and nothing in the table is closer, so the two ends are untested inside that band. That is why the face publishes an `ambiguity_band` per substitute (numeric ends only -- a boolean end has no distance to a line) and why "0 differences" must never be reported without it: two substitutes that never disagree have only been compared where disagreeing was impossible.

> Three-way reading rule (the card asked "disclosure or change of meaning"): a substitute is a **disclosure** only if it is exact on the moved set *and* answers the guard the same way on every other comparison; **exact but different elsewhere** is a change of meaning that happens to agree today; **not exact** is unusable. Score all three, publish them side by side, and let the verdict name which substitute you may act on -- "the table is enough" and "the tight end of the table is enough" are different instructions.

Engineering pits born here: (1) the first fixtures put the pooled end at 1.9 against a 2.0 threshold and asserted it read the row as inside -- 1.9 < 2.0 is below, so the *assertion* was wrong and three legs failed on correct code (r1281 shape, third sighting); (2) `published_verdict_wide` is not carried on E266's comparison records, it lives on the source rows, so the boolean variant silently scored `undefined` on all 36 comparisons until it was joined back by row index -- and the "agreement" block reported 0 judged rows, which is the only reason it was noticed (an undefined population that reads as "no disagreements" is the r1261 both-sides-equal shape one field over); (3) a verdict branch that reads a variable defined later in `run()` is a NameError only at run time, not at import, so `verify` is the leg that catches ordering, not `selftest`.

Evidence: scripts/e268_screen_on_pooled_end.py (selftest 41/41, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDPOOLED-2026-10-29.json (verdict=a_pooled_group_end_runs_the_screen; 36 comparisons / 2 moves / 4 groups; guarded tight pooled end 24 below t / 12 above, 0 disagreements; nearest gap 0.0835), source face BANDTRANSFER-2026-10-29 (E262), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1294-e268-pooled-end.md.


## E269 -- the tight end cannot transfer badly because on this population it cannot move anything; an inert zero is not a clean transfer

> Every arm in E259 publishes a p05 as well as a p95 and every row a `verdict_tight`, so the tight half of E262's transfer question had never been scored -- and it is not implied by the wide answer (the wide end decides rejections on the side a row already sits beyond, the tight end decides over-crediting, and the two come from opposite tails of the same stream). On the identical 48 ordered pairs: the wide end moves **2** verdicts, the tight end moves **0**, and the pooled minimum p05 (what "use the tightest" adopts) moves **0** too -- while the tight verdict is the *stricter* one (10 of 12 rows outside their tight band against 8 of 12 outside their wide band) and windows disagree about their tight tail by up to **10.08%**.

> A zero here is worthless as evidence unless it says which zero it is. Publish per row the **multiplier at which the verdict flips** (`flip_multiplier`: band is `(lo*m, hi*m)`, so "outside" reduces to `m < m_flip` on the side the row sits on) and compare it with the range of p05 values that row's group actually published. All 12 rows sit at least **13.5%** outside the widest swing their group contains, and 0 rows could move at any published p05 -- so the verdict is `the_tight_end_is_inert_on_this_population`, and the tight half is **untested**, not safe. The operational instruction narrows rather than widens: **do not borrow the wide end** (those are E262's 2 moves); nothing on this table argues against borrowing the tight end, and nothing argues for it either.

> Disclosure worth its own line: in `cross:200` all four windows publish **exactly** p05 = 1.0000, i.e. the tight tail is degenerate in that group while the wide tail is not. A degenerate end cannot transfer at all, and reporting "0 moves" for it as if it were agreement would be an artefact of no variation, not of robustness.

> Reading rule that generalises: whenever an equivalence / "no move" / "nothing changes" result is published, it must be paired with (a) an activity proof that the mechanism ran, and (b) a distance proof -- how far the nearest observation sits from the point where the answer would flip, in the units of the variation actually available. Without (b), "0 of 48" is indistinguishable from "could not have been otherwise".

Engineering pits born here: (1) BANDTRANSFER's `rows` are E262's resolved records, not raw source rows -- re-running `e262.row_records` on them marks all 16 unjudgeable for a missing `band_draws`, and the face cheerfully published a verdict over 0 measured rows; `verify` re-derived the same wrong answer, so only the printed run output caught it (check that a verdict's population is non-empty before believing it); (2) a comprehension filter referencing its own loop variable (`d` inside its own `for ... if d is not None`) is a run-time NameError that compiles clean -- `verify` cannot see it either; (3) a selftest fixture placed the flip exactly on the boundary (`-0.45` vs `-0.3*1.5`), where binary floating point puts it below the edge, so a correct implementation "failed" -- move the fixture off the tie, never loosen the leg (r1281 family, fourth sighting).

Evidence: scripts/e269_tight_end_transfer.py (selftest 35/35, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDTIGHT-2026-10-29.json (verdict=the_tight_end_is_inert_on_this_population; 48 pairs / 0 tight moves / 2 wide moves; 0 rows could move at any published p05; nearest flip 13.5% outside the range), source faces BANDWINDIST-2026-10-29 (E259) + BANDTRANSFER-2026-10-29 (E262), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1295-e269-tight-end.md.


## E270 -- a screen's reach is what the published faces carry, and presence is not agreement

> E267/E268's guard consumes four per-row numbers (b, band_lo, band_hi, own_p95). This audit walks
> every dated BAND* face and asks which of them actually publish those four -- the rule being
> published is not the same thing as the rule being re-runnable from the tables.

**Reading.** 18 dated faces, 86 record collections, 25 collections carry at least one guard input,
but only 4 carry the FULL triple on every record they measure: 72 record-readings (3 of the 4
collections on measured rows only -- unmeasured rows legitimately hold None in the very fields the
join checks). Against that, 27 verdict-bearing collections (584 records) publish a judgement with
none of the four. So the screen is a table recipe on the faces that carry the triple and a black
box everywhere else -- `guard_inputs_are_face_local`.

**The cross-check, which is the load-bearing half.** Presence is not agreement: the same row index
appears in six faces and its own_p95 could be six different numbers. Joining 216 records to the
canonical `/rows` collection of the face that published them compares 420 shared guard cells:
420 agree, 0 disagree, max |diff| 0.0. The family's problem is therefore COVERAGE, not
inconsistency -- and that distinction cannot be made by counting fields.

**Disclosures that keep the census honest.** (i) `b` is two different quantities in this family:
the row's own move, and the clearance curves' buffer grid (9 collections). Buffer grids are named
separately (`b_without_a_band`) and kept out of the row census, or a buffer sweep of 43 values
reads as 43 half-instrumented rows. (ii) The domain excludes the `_latest.json` mirrors (byte
copies of a dated face) and the study's own output -- a second burn would otherwise audit the audit
and answer differently, which is exactly the r1238 self-inclusion defect. (iii) A record without an
`index` is counted as unjoined, never dropped; `unjoined` is published beside `joined`.

**Pit.** The first burn published `canonical: none` with 0 cells compared, because `canon_map`
required a collection whose EVERY record carried all four inputs -- but unmeasured rows hold None
in exactly those fields, so the canonical face was rejected in favour of nothing and the value
cross-check silently measured zero cells while the verdict still read as a coverage finding. The
rule is now "the collection with the most complete records", and the standard error of that
mistake is visible: the face publishes `canonical_basis` and `cells_compared`.

**Second pit (a count that moves is not a re-derivable count).** The domain grew mid-round -- a
downstream leg published `BANDPATH-2026-10-30.json` while this face was being written -- and every
total moved (17 -> 18 faces, 536 -> 584 records). A scan whose input is a directory must publish
the inventory it measured and re-derive over THAT list: `verify` now takes `source_faces` as its
scope and reports a domain that has grown or shrunk as a notice ("re-run to republish"), never as a
silent change of the published numbers.

Evidence: scripts/e270_guard_field_audit.py (selftest 29/29, verify 0 problems),
results/state_tilt/BANDFIELDS-2026-10-29.json (verdict=guard_inputs_are_face_local; 17 faces,
4 guard-complete collections / 72 record-readings, 26 verdict collections without inputs / 536
records, 420 of 420 joined cells agree max |diff| 0.0), S6 leg `guard_field_audit`,
digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1296-e270-guard-field-audit.md.

## E273 -- a threshold replaces the triple exactly, but only with its rule attached

E270 measured the family's reach: the guard consumes `b`, `band_lo`, `band_hi`, `own_p95`, only 4 of
17 published collections carry all four, and 27 verdict-bearing collections (584 records) publish a
judgement a reader cannot re-decide. But every rule here is `multiplier vs threshold` --
`t_max_end = |b|/max(|lo|,|hi|)` is EXACT (`outside(m) <=> m < t`), `t_side = |b|/|own-side edge|`
is the form S3 was fitted on -- so the band is redundant arithmetic *if the published threshold is
that band's threshold*. Re-deriving on the 36 comparisons that publish both spellings: residual
0.0 / 0.0, the literal band test agrees with `m < t_max_end` on 36/36, the side test with
`m < t_side` on 36/36, and all three published screens (S1 single / S2 guarded / S3 bracket)
re-run from threshold columns alone at 36/36 with **zero** band columns consulted. Reach: 9
collections / 120 records that E270 called not-guard-runnable are threshold-runnable (BANDMARGIN
`/comparison_margins`, BANDPOOLED `/comparisons` + its four `mislabelled` sub-collections,
BANDSCREEN's three secondary collections). The substitute is exact, so the missing triple is a
documentation gap, not a barrier -- but 18 of 36 rows publish two DIFFERENT thresholds and 6 of
those read a different verdict on them (1 flips the guarded screen), so a threshold without the
face's rule label is ambiguous on 16.7% of the population. Rule of use: publish `t_max_end` (the
exact form) beside `own_p95`/`donor_p95`, and if you publish `t_side` instead, name which screen it
belongs to.

**Pit.** `census()` was right and my selftest expectation was wrong: the fixture published two
threshold collections, not one. A leg that widens the code to match a hand-typed expectation is how
a detector stops detecting -- the fix went into L17/L18. Sibling, guarded by construction: `verify`
re-derives from the sources, never from its own summary (L20 pins that a doctored `rederivation`
block is caught), because a verdict that lives only in a face's summary is not a gate (r1266).

Evidence: scripts/e273_guard_from_threshold.py (selftest 20/20, verify 0 problems),
results/state_tilt/BANDTHRESHGUARD-2026-10-29.json (verdict=
threshold_substitutes_for_the_triple_only_alongside_its_rule; 36 comparisons, residual 0.0/0.0,
rules 36/36 exact, 18 rows with two thresholds / 6 own-verdict ambiguous / 1 guarded ambiguous,
9 newly threshold-runnable collections / 120 records), S6 leg `guard_from_threshold`,
digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1297-e273-threshold-guard.md.


## E274 -- a donor axis is decisive only for the rows whose flip multiplier sits inside the
spread the group offers

E262 published 48 ordered (donor, recipient) pairs and every consumer since (E266/E267/E268) read
them one donor at a time, so a reader of a single recipient could not tell whether the finding was
"do not borrow" or "do not borrow from THIS cell". Sweeping every donor end each (leg, base) group
offers -- own cell included as the control, which reproduces the published verdict on 12/12 rows --
answers it on the same published numbers: 3 of 4 groups are donor-invariant, and the one that is not
(cross:60) moves 2 of its 6 rows under exactly one donor, `all_five` (p95 2.2963, which is also
E262's published dominator there). 15 of the 16 donor ends move nothing.

**The mechanism is two published numbers, not a re-run.** A row only moves when its flip multiplier
`m_flip` (= b/band_lo on the negative side) falls inside the p95 spread the group actually offers;
cross:60 offers [1.9678, 2.2963] and the two movers sit at 2.1965 / 2.1384, while every other group
straddles nothing (spreads 9.1-16.8%) and nothing moves. So the measurable content of "the donor
matters" is "this row's flip multiplier is inside this group's spread", and the pivotal cell is
simply whichever end lies beyond it.

**Corollary that changes an instruction.** The published pair choice (the group's dominator) is the
LEAST conservative donor in the only group where the axis is live -- it is the single donor that
overturns verdicts, while all three narrow ends preserve them. A table that highlights its dominator
is therefore highlighting its most aggressive borrow, not a safe one; conservative means the
narrowest end.

**Pit.** The face's first `verdict_of` divided a per-group count by the foreign-pair count and read
"15 of 16 donor ends move nothing" off a mixed denominator; it now publishes donor_ends and
donor_ends_moving_a_row separately, because "donor-row pairs" and "donor ends" are different
populations and the whole sentence is about the second. Sibling: the own-cell donor must stay in the
sweep as a control -- drop it and "0 moves" becomes untestable.

Evidence: scripts/e271_donor_choice_sensitivity.py (selftest 22/22, verify 0 problems),
results/state_tilt/BANDDONORCHOICE-2026-10-29.json (verdict=
donor_choice_matters_do_not_borrow_from_this_cell; 12 measured rows / 4 groups / 36 foreign pairs;
2 rows moved, both straddlers; pivotal cross:60=all_five), S6 leg `donor_choice_sensitivity`,
digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1298-e271-donor-choice.md.

## E275 -- a flip multiplier plus the range an axis offers predicts, in advance, whether that axis can move a row -- and the predicted set is the one the faces published

> Card number vs pool id: this study ran as pool entry E274-SPREAD-STRADDLE-SWEEP; the card is E275 because E274 was already assigned to the r1298 donor-axis card by a concurrent seat. Pool ids and card ids drift in this repo and are recorded separately.

> A mechanism becomes a screen only when it is scored on more than the one axis it was found on. E271 showed the donor axis is decisive exactly on rows whose flip multiplier sits inside the p95 spread their group offers; this face walks the whole BAND* family on the three axes that publish **both** a range and a moved set (wide_donor = group p95 spread vs BANDDONORCHOICE's moved rows; tight_p05 = group p05 spread vs BANDTIGHT's could-move rows; top_ladder = the row's own multiplier span vs BANDTOPFLIP's movement-dependent rows). The four-way reading (inside / near_edge / outside / untested) reproduces **every** published moved set exactly: **4 moved observations, 4 hits, 0 missed, 0 flagged-but-inert** on 12 measured rows.

> The reading rule: **"do not borrow from this cell" is decidable from two published numbers** (`m_flip`, the offered range) without re-running any sweep -- but only as far as the moved observations reach. 4 is above the 3-positive floor and still 12 rows on one book, so the verdict carries its own power caveat, and a flip within 5% of the range width is published as `near_edge` rather than counted as a decided `inside`.

> The pit is the family's recurring one: **same name, different quantity**. BANDTOPFLIP publishes `flipped_ids` ("flips at EVERY measurement", empty) beside `depends_ids` ("at SOME", 2 rows); the first cut scored the former -- it reads like "the rows that moved" -- and would have published `the_screen_is_unsafe_on_some_axis` off a lookup error rather than a measurement. Fix pattern: carry **both** sets and publish their arithmetic gap (`moves_only_in_the_weaker_set`) so the choice is auditable; then pin it with a leg whose fixture has a row that moves sometimes but not always.

> Two smaller generalisations: a **join key shape is part of the contract** (published ids are `source/cell/row`; a `source/row` key silently matches nothing and reads exactly like a failing screen), and a **zero-width range cannot decide anything** -- `straddle(m, 3.0, 3.0)` must read `untested`, not `inside`, because a single point offers no spread to be inside of.

Evidence: scripts/e274_spread_straddle_sweep.py (selftest 29/29, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDSTRADDLESWEEP-2026-10-29.json (verdict=two_published_numbers_predict_every_scored_axis; 12 rows x 3 axes, 4 moved observations, 4 hits), S6 leg `spread_straddle_sweep` (rc=0, 0.16s), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1299-e274-straddle-sweep.md.

## E276 -- "this tail is inert" is a statement about the published multipliers, not about the tail: put both tails on one ruler before spending draw budget

> Card number vs pool id: this study ran as pool entry E272-TIGHT-FLIP-BUDGET; the card is E276 because pool ids and card ids have drifted apart in this repo (pool id E272 was already used by an earlier atlas pair).

> A zero on one tail is only a finding if the OTHER tail can move something. E269 published the flip multiplier of every row and found the nearest one 13.5% outside the widest p05 swing its group publishes; that is a tight-half budget. E272 puts the wide half on the SAME number -- one m_flip per row, imported from E269 rather than re-implemented -- and measures each tail by how much room it actually offers: the p05 range vs the p95 range across the windows sharing the row's (leg, base count).

> The ruler that makes the two comparable is gap / that tail's own spread ("how many spreads of draw budget before this tail could matter"). Tight normalised-gap median 5.14 spreads vs wide 1.22; the wide tail is closer on 10 of 12 rows and is the only measurable tail on 2 more (where p05 is 1.0000 on all four windows). The tight end never wins on a row it can actually move.

> Polarity decides reachability, and it is published per row. A flip above 1 needs a LARGER multiplier (widening -- the wide tail); below 1 needs a smaller one (narrowing -- the tight tail). 10 of 12 flips need widening while every published p05 in the family is >= 1.0000, so no published p05 can re-enter any row: the tight end is inert by construction of the published multipliers, which is exactly why "the tight end transferred cleanly" was never the right reading of E269's zero.

> A zero gap is necessary but not sufficient for a move. e257.outside is strict, so a flip sitting exactly on a published end is still inside; the face publishes reachable and reachable_strict separately and only the strict set feeds the verdict. Soundness is then checked against the other face: the wide-reachable set must contain every row E262 actually moved -- here it equals it (rows 9 and 13), and verify fails if they diverge.

> A spread of zero is unmeasurable, never infinite. cross:200 publishes p05 = 1.0000 on all four windows; dividing a gap by that spread would print an infinite budget and rank that tail first. Those readings are reported as unmeasurable with a reason, and whichever tail remains measurable is named in closer_note rather than assumed.

Evidence: scripts/e272_flip_budget_two_tails.py (selftest 39/39, verify 0 problems), results/state_tilt/BANDFLIPBUDGET-2026-10-29.json (verdict=the_wide_tail_is_the_only_tail_that_can_reach_a_row; 12 measured rows, wide-reachable [9, 13] = E262's moved set, tight-reachable []), S6 leg flip_budget_two_tails (rc=0, 0.15s), digest research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1300-e272-flip-budget.md.

## E277 -- a cleared screen row is not equally cleared: publish the margin the offered range has already spent, and say which zone it is in

> Card number vs pool id: this study ran as pool entry `E275-SCREEN-MARGIN-BUDGET`; the card is
> E277 because E275 and E276 were already assigned by the r1299 and r1300 windows. Pool ids and
> card ids drift in this repo and are recorded separately.

> An exact screen is not a finished instruction. E274 scored the straddle flag against every moved
> set the band family published and it reproduced all of them (**4 moved observations, 4 hits, 0
> missed, 0 flagged-but-inert**), so a reader can now decide "do not borrow from this cell" from
> two published numbers. What that reading does **not** say is how much room a cleared row has
> left: `outside` covers a row whose flip sits 6% above the widest multiplier its group ever
> offered and a row whose flip sits 45% above it, and the two are different instructions.

> **The budget is one ratio.** For a measured row, `budget_spent = hi / m_flip` where `hi` is the
> widest multiplier the row's (leg, base) group actually offers and `m_flip` is the multiplier at
> which the row's verdict flips. It is the share of the way from "no perturbation" (1.0) to the
> flip that the group's widest offer already travels; `room_left = 1 - budget_spent`. Both are
> functions of published numbers — no draws, no panel, no engine call.

> **"Cleared" is five zones, and two of them mean opposite things.** `spent_by_build` is a row
> whose flip sits at or below the group's **tightest** offered multiplier: it is not nearly spent,
> it is spent before the budget starts, so a slightly wider perturbation cannot be what moves it.
> `spent` is a row outside the range whose widest end already reaches >= 90% of the flip. Keeping
> them in one "at risk" bucket loses the only distinction the budget adds.

> Reading (12 measured rows, one book): 2 straddle, 4 spent_by_build, 2 spent, 4 open. The
> straddle zone **is** the guard screen's moved set `{9, 13}`; the open rows have spent 54.7%,
> 65.9%, 73.7% and 81.8% of their threshold while the spent rows have spent 93.4% and 96.5%. None
> of the six near-spent rows is named by BANDNEAR1's `near_one_dependent_rows` (empty) or by
> BANDMARGIN's guard moves (exactly the two straddlers), so the budget names rows nothing else
> flags — it is neither a restatement nor corroboration.

> **What the zone is not.** It is a statement about the published range, not a movement
> prediction, and that is pinned rather than claimed: none of the six near-spent rows moved in the
> published donor sweep. `spent_by_build` is the sharpest case — the tightest offer already passes
> the flip and the row still did not move, because the sweep moves a specific borrowed quantity,
> not the bare multiplier. Publish the zone and the non-prediction together or the next reader
> treats it as a second screen.

Evidence: `scripts/e275_screen_margin_budget.py` (selftest 25/25, verify 0 problems),
`results/state_tilt/BANDSCREENBUDGET-2026-10-29.json`
(verdict=`cleared_is_not_one_reading_the_budget_names_rows_nothing_else_flags`; 12 rows:
4 open / 2 spent / 4 spent_by_build / 2 straddles), S6 leg `screen_margin_budget` (rc=0, 0.14s),
smoke leg `a cleared row is not equally cleared` (1/1 PASS standalone), digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1301-e275-screen-margin-budget.md`.

## E278 -- a floor that cannot move is a property of the BAND BUILD, not of the windows: census every published lower end, then re-read the same stream through a different band rule

E272 put both tails of the flip budget on one ruler and found the tight tail reaching none of the 12
measured rows, because every published p05 in the family is >= 1.0000 while 10 of 12 flips need a
multiplier LARGER than that.  "The tight end never narrows" is a claim about windows, and it is
decidable without a single new draw.

What the build actually does, read off the source rather than assumed: `BAND_PCT = (0.0, 100.0)` and
`lo = vals[floor(pct/100 * (n-1))]`, so **lo is the MINIMUM of the per-draw coefficient** over a
NESTED prefix.  The minimum of a growing sample can only move outward, so |lo| is monotone
non-decreasing in draws and m = |lo|(top) / |lo|(base) cannot fall below 1 for base < top whenever the
extreme sits on the negative side.  The endpoint's own draw exponent is already published
(BANDDRAW: gamma 0.348 head / 0.647 tail, endpoint rose on 6 of 7 rungs with a minimum rise of 0.0%),
which is the same statement measured rather than derived.

The census, on every published BAND* face on disk: **140 multiplier lower ends (68 p05 + 72 range
lows), not one below 1.0, 39 exactly 1.0.**  The exact ones are not a window that narrowed and then
stopped -- they are the degenerate branch (the extremum arrived inside the base prefix), and
BANDNEAR1 already publishes the proof: drop one seed and those rows lift to 1.11..1.20.  The
counterfactual closes it: the SAME synthetic stream read as a 5% band yields m = 0.922, so the floor
comes from the rule, and a percentile band would revive every tight-end question the family has been
answering with zeros.

Three reusable pieces:

> when a measurement sits exactly on a floor, ask whether the floor is reachable at all -- write the
> statistic's definition (which index, of what, over which sample) and check whether the floor is a
> property of the DEFINITION.  A tail that can only ever return zero is not evidence about the world;
> publishing it repeatedly manufactures a finding out of an identity.
> the counterfactual must run on the same stream: rerunning a different sample with a different rule
> confounds two changes, and the only clean reading is one sample through two rules (here extremum
> band m = 1.000 vs 5% band m = 0.922).
> publish the branch that would falsify you -- the monotonicity holds only while the extreme is
> negative; an all-positive draw stream shrinks |min| and m < 1 becomes reachable.  Carrying that
> branch as a named alternative (with a leg that exercises it) is what keeps the verdict scoped
> instead of absolute.

Two pits caught in the same round: (1) the first census walked the `*_latest` MIRRORS beside their
dated twins and counted 136 p05 where there are 68 -- a family census must exclude mirrors explicitly
and list them; (2) the face's own counterfactual first returned m = 1.0000 for the *extremum* leg
because the synthetic gaussian happened to put its minimum inside the base prefix, i.e. the very
degeneracy the face is about -- strictness needed a stream whose extreme arrives after the base, and
degeneracy needed its own separate assertion.

Evidence: `scripts/e277_tight_multiplier_floor.py` (selftest 23/23, verify 0 problems),
`results/state_tilt/BANDFLOOR-2026-10-29.json`
(verdict=`tight_end_dead_by_construction_family_should_stop_publishing_tight_pass_checks`; 140 lower
ends, 0 below 1.0, 39 exactly 1.0; counterfactual 5% band m=0.922), S6 leg `tight_multiplier_floor`
(rc=0, 0.11s), smoke leg `the tight multiplier floor is the band build` (1/1 PASS standalone), digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1302-e277-tight-multiplier-floor.md`.

## E279 -- a zero-spread tail is a hole in a NORMALISED ruler: censused by base count it is the floor landing where the percentile has least support, so publish "unmeasurable" and never a default

E272 published one ruler for both tails: normalised gap = gap_pct / that tail's own spread.  The
ruler is undefined when the spread is exactly 0, and cross:200 was exactly that (p05 = 1.0000 on all
four windows), stranding 2 published rows.  "One group can be bad luck" is decidable without a new
draw: census every published arm-table group at both tails and ask whether the zeros cluster.

Census (16 arm rows -> 4 (leg, base) groups x 4 cells): **3 of 4 groups measurable at both tails.  The
single zero spread is cross:200's tight tail, and all four of its cells sit on the 1.0 floor.**  The
floor's reach is what explains it, not the group: **8 of 16 published tight values are exactly 1.0,
and 7 of those 8 are at base 200** (base 60 contributes 1).  A thin shuffle across few base counts
leaves the percentile with almost no support, so its cells collapse onto the floor together -- the
hole is E277's build property showing up where resolution is lowest, and a 60-window group never
spreads to zero at all.  The wide tail is clean: no zero anywhere, smallest spread 9.08%.

So the reading is not "the ruler broke on one group"; it is "the tight tail's spread is a function of
the shuffle depth, and at base 200 it can reach exactly 0".  The published policy carries that:
a group whose tail spread is 0 is flagged, and a row in it stays unmeasured rather than being given a
default; a group flagged on BOTH tails has no usable ruler at all.

Two reusable pieces:

> normalise only by a quantity that can be nonzero, and publish the degenerate branch as
> UNMEASURABLE.  Substituting a default (other tail, pooled spread, 1.0) turns "we could not read
> this" into a reading, and the substitution is invisible in the table.
> when a degenerate cell appears, census its neighbours before calling it luck: 1 zero in 4 groups
> looks like an outlier until you count where the underlying floor sits (7 of 8 floor hits at one
> base count).  The concentration is the diagnosis.

Two pits caught in the same round: (1) a group with ONE published cell has min == max by construction,
so a naive `spread == 0` test flags it as a zero spread -- counting "nothing to compare" as evidence
of a hole; the selftest fixture caught it before publish and the class is now explicit
(`single_cell_group`, never `zero_spread`).  (2) one cell publishing two different values must poison
the group (`conflicting_cell_values`) rather than quietly taking one of them -- otherwise the ruler is
built on an arbitrary choice of duplicate.

Evidence: `scripts/e278_spread_floor.py` (selftest 13/13, verify 0 problems),
`results/state_tilt/BANDSPREADFLOOR-2026-10-29.json`
(verdict=`the_zero_spread_tail_is_the_band_floor_landing_on_the_thin_shuffle`; 4 groups, zero at
cross:200 tight only, 8/16 tight values at the floor, wide min spread 9.08%, 2 rows stranded), S6 leg
`spread_floor` (rc=0, <1s), smoke leg `the one zero-spread tail is the band floor at the thin
shuffle` (1/1 PASS standalone), digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1303-e278-spread-floor.md`.

## E280 -- "these two faces disagree" is not a finding until both were priced on the same bars: one extra bar moves the point estimate and every shuffled band

The chain leg `star_self_price` went red at r1303. E252's verify reported the star's cross
coefficient as -0.7252014696754883 against E251's published -0.7250430277727764, and a field diff
said **177 leaves moved** -- including the shuffled band (`band_star_lag1.hi` 0.2357 -> 0.3514).
The seeded hypothesis was that r1277's star-rule refactor changed how the shared draw stream is
consumed, i.e. that a published band had been silently re-randomised. That hypothesis is **false**,
and measurement says so in two independent ways:

1. **Published bytes, same vintage.** `STAROWN-2026-10-29.json` and `STARSELF-2026-10-29.json`
   carry the same number to the last digit: b1 = b_cross = -0.7250430277727764, abs diff 0.0.
2. **One panel, both implementations.** Run E251's cell and E252's cell in one process on today's
   panel (1329 sessions): b1 = b_cross = -0.7252014696754883, **abs diff 0.0**. They are the same
   regression, not two.

What moved is the **vintage**: 1328 -> 1329 sessions. `starown_latest.json` had been advanced to the
10-30 face by an unrelated chain run, while E252's face still sat on 10-29, and the verify compared
them across that boundary. The 177 "drifted" fields are one extra bar propagating through a
200-draw max-statistic band -- not a stream change.

Repair (rule D1, declared in the runner before the numbers were read): the identity is a
**same-panel** statement, so the gate now prefers `STAROWN-<the face's own cutoff>` and, when only a
newer vintage exists, publishes `vintage_lag` and refuses to call the two implementations different.
No face was reburned; no draw stream was restored -- both repairs on the card were unnecessary.

Second deliverable, which outlives this case: the RNG pin is a **property, not a number**.
`own_column_band` with the same (panel, star, draws, seed) reproduces the same band, and seed+1
moves it; the selftest asserts both directions, and the first version of the leg was **vacuous**
with 8 draws because `_band` returns `band=None` below 20 draws -- "same input, same band" was
true because both sides had no band. The leg now requires `measurable` before it can pass.

Evidence: `scripts/e280_e251_rng_drift_repin.py` (selftest 9/9),
`results/state_tilt/STAROWNREPIN-2026-10-30.json` (branch D1, same-panel identity 0.0,
177 moved leaves, band pinned), `scripts/e252_star_prices_itself.py` verify (vintage-aware, selftest
21/21), S6 leg `star_own_rng_repin`, smoke legs
`product: the star's own row is priced against ...` (vintage-aware) and
`product: a claimed RNG drift is decided by measurement, and the stream is pinned`, digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1304-e280-rng-drift-repin.md`.

## E281 -- an agreement the other side could not have avoided is not evidence: when one tail is degenerate, "they agree" measures nothing

E278's policy said: when a tail's spread is 0, "read the other tail". E279 tested it on the 12
measurable rows of E272's two-tail budget and found **2 substitution events, 0 contradictions, 2
inflations** -- and every one of the 2 agreements is **vacuous**. The stranded tail publishes a
degenerate multiplier range (`min == max == 1.0`), so it is mechanically unable to reach any flip;
its "unreachable" is a property of the build, not a reading. The substitute therefore had nothing to
contradict, and the rows that needed the policy carry **no evidence** that the policy is sound.

The general rule: **when one side of a comparison is degenerate, agreement on those units cannot
support a soundness claim.** Split the counts into *informatively agreeing* and *vacuously agreeing*
and publish both; a policy that was never exercised reads exactly like a policy that passed. This is
the same shape as r1261's equivalence leg, which passed because neither arm had traded.

Second half of the card: substitution here is **monotone**, and monotonicity is measurable. The swap
view names the same 2 rows in both directions (tight->wide adds the claim on 2 of 12; wide->tight
removes it on the same 2), and `wide_dominates_tight_violations = []`. So a substituted reading is an
**upper bound**: it can prove a row *can* move and can never prove it *cannot*. Publish the row set,
not just the two counts -- "inflates 2 / deflates 2" without the set identity invites the false
reading of two independent events.

Scope: with n=2 agree and n=2 disagree, the bracket is `(0.0, 2.0327]` with `calibrated = false`, and
the disagreement is exactly where the substitute's normalised gap is 0.0 (it sits on the flip).
Published as an interval so nobody reads "X = 1.0" as validated.

Evidence: `scripts/e279_substitution_soundness.py` (selftest 26/26),
`results/state_tilt/BANDSUBSTITUTE-2026-10-29.json` (2 events, 0 deflations, 2 vacuous; 24/24
identity to E272; stranded set == E278's `["cross:200"]`), S6 leg `substitution_soundness`, smoke leg
`product: reading the other tail never contradicts ...`, digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1305-e279-substitution.md`.

## E282 -- ask whether the policy is LOAD-BEARING, not whether it is sound: a dependency audit is a scope test on published conclusions, and its natural output is a defect in the face it audits

E279 proved the substitution policy is sound as an upper bound and unproven as a reading, then scoped
it with "substitute only to prove a row CAN move, never to conclude it cannot". That scoping is only
harmless if no **already-published** conclusion needs the forbidden direction. So the follow-up is not
another soundness test -- it is a dependency audit: walk every dated face in the family, extract each
`(face, row, tail)` reachability claim **structurally** (a node carrying both tail blocks with a
multiplier range), and ask of every `cannot`: is its own tail stranded, and does the face text rest on
it?

Five definitions make the audit decidable, and each one exists to stop a specific false answer.

1. **Claim unit is structural, never nominal.** A bare `reachable` key is not a claim; the pair of
   tail blocks is. In this family 27 dated faces were scanned and exactly **1** carries the pair (24
   claims). The other 26 speak in prose and are *disclosure-only* -- they cannot be dependency-checked
   at all, which is itself the finding: a conclusion stated in prose is unauditable by construction.
2. **Dependent = a `cannot` whose own tail is stranded.** Measured: 22 of 24 claims are `cannot`, but
   only **2** of them rest on a stranded tail -- the rest are measurements of a live interval, which
   no substitution touches. The count that matters is 2, not 22.
3. **Load-bearing = the face text names that tail AND carries a negative marker AND publishes no
   `can` on that same tail.** This is what turns "dependent" into "a conclusion rests on it". Here it
   is **0**: the only face holding those claims already says the tail is inert because the population
   never publishes a narrowing multiplier, *not because the tail is safe*.
4. **Self-disclosure clears the flag, and the disclosure is recorded.** Three faces independently
   already publish the vacuity (inert / dead by construction / untested rather than safe). So the
   policy is load-bearing exactly where the family had already said the claim is vacuous -- no
   withdrawal needed, and no `cannot` on a stranded tail may ever be read as a measurement.
5. **A defect found in a published face is disclosed and seeded, never repaired in the round that
   found it.** The finding round must not also be the round that re-burns the face it is judging.

That fifth rule earned its place immediately: the audit re-derived **24/24** of E279's census booleans
and its stranded set, and in doing so found that E279's summary field
`rows_where_tails_disagree_on_reachability` is keyed on the **group label** while the disagreement is
**cell-scoped**. `cross` has 4 cells and exactly 1 disagreeing cell, `star_lag1_residual` likewise --
so the field names a whole group for one cell. It is not wrong about *which groups* contain a
disagreement; it over-claims at group scope, and a reader cannot recover the cells from it. That is the
same-name-different-quantity family as E240/E253, and it is invisible from the group-level digest prose
(r1305 wrote the cells correctly; only the machine-readable field is lossy).

Two reusable lessons. **(a)** "Is this policy safe?" is the wrong question once a policy has been
scoped; ask "does anything already published depend on it?" -- a dependency audit is a scope test over
conclusions, and it is cheap because it reads faces, not draws. **(b)** The best thing a cell-by-cell
identity check can produce is a defect in the face it audits: agreement is what makes the audit
trustworthy, and disagreement is what makes it worth running. Publish both, and seed the repair
separately so the finding round is never the verifying round.

Evidence: `scripts/e281_substitution_dependency_audit.py` (selftest 18/18, run/verify green),
`results/state_tilt/BANDSUBSTITUTEAUDIT-2026-10-29.json` (27 faces / 24 claims / 2 dependent /
0 load-bearing; identity 24/24, stranded set and disagreement set both agree with E279's census;
E279 summary field ambiguous with per-group counts 1-of-4), S6 leg
`substitution_dependency_audit` (0.19s), smoke leg `product: a cannot on a stranded tail needs no
withdrawal here ...`, repair card E284-DISAGREEMENT-FIELD-SCOPE, digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1306-e281-dependency-audit.md`.
## E283 -- a statistic that is clamped cannot answer a question about position: read the clamp, then measure the position

E279 bracketed the substitution threshold from two disagreeing rows and left a hypothesis: both sat at
a dominant-tail **normalised gap of exactly 0.0**, so perhaps every disagreement is a *rounding boundary
artefact* rather than a distance effect. The census said no -- but the interesting part is **why the
hypothesis could never have been true**, and that reason is reusable.

**First: the gap field is clamped.** Upstream computes `gap_pct` as a distance *from the range*, and
returns **exactly `0.0` for any flip inside it**. So `normalised_gap == 0` is true for **every interior
reading**, not just for one sitting on the flip. Reading it as "the substitute lands on the flip" is a
fallback masquerading as a measurement: the field cannot express the question being asked of it. The
census re-measured on `p = (flip − lo)/(hi − lo)` and found the two cells at **p = 0.696 / 0.519**,
strictly interior, with the other tail **48–50 pct** away.

**Second: a boundary-only disagreement is excluded by the contract that produced it.** `reachable` is
defined as `gap ≤ TOL`, so a non-reaching tail's gap is **strictly greater than `TOL` by construction**.
Two verdicts produced by one contract with one tolerance cannot differ *only* on the inclusive edge --
that branch is unreachable, not merely unobserved. Two independent grounds, both published as measured
identities on the face rather than asserted in prose, and both are one line in a selftest.

**Third: scope is a number, not an adjective.** "Family-wide" turned out to be **1 qualifying face of
55** (`BANDFLIPBUDGET`) and 12 rows: 54 files publish prose or verdicts and carry neither tail's range.
Publishing the qualifying/excluded split stops a census of one face from being read as a census of the
family, and the `_latest` mirrors had to be dropped **by name** -- counting them censused the same cells
twice and doubled every count on the first run.

**Fourth: the surviving disagreement is not noise, it is geometry.** The two tails' ranges are
**disjoint intervals**, not nested ones (tight `[1.000, 1.101]` vs wide `[1.968, 2.296]` on `cross:60`),
so disagreement simply means the flip landed in one band and not the other. And the wide band is not a
sweep: two rows on the same face fall **inside the inter-range gap** and are unreachable by **both**
tails -- headroom the widening spends without resolving anything, which is the next card.

That fourth rule earned its place immediately: the two rows are invisible from any per-tail summary,
because each tail is internally consistent about them; only the *gap between the ranges* shows that the
widening was spent for nothing.

Two reusable lessons. **(a)** Before testing a hypothesis with a published statistic, ask whether that
statistic is **monotone or clamped** over the region where the hypothesis lives: a clamped field reads
the same value across the entire interior, so agreement with it is vacuous in the same way E281's
degenerate tail was. **(b)** When two verdicts are produced by one contract, disagreements can only come
from where the contract's inputs differ -- publish that region (here, the inter-range gap) and the
"is this a boundary artefact" question answers itself without a threshold.

Evidence: `scripts/e282_substitution_disagreement_census.py` (selftest 23/23, run/verify green),
`results/state_tilt/BANDDISAGREE-2026-10-29.json` (1/55 faces qualifying, 12 rows, 2 disagreement cells
at position 0.696/0.519 with the tight tail 48.5/49.9 pct away, gap 0 on 2/2 reaching readings = clamped,
boundary tie impossible in principle), S6 leg `substitution_disagreement_census` (0.17s), smoke leg
`product: the two disagreeing tails are a RANGE difference …`, digest
`research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1307-e282-disagreement-census.md`, next card
`E285-INTERRANGE-GAP-CEILING`.

## E286 -- a test whose failure mode needs a tolerance that destroys the test has not been run

E279 declared its contradiction branch (the substitute *deflates* the conclusion) and reported
`events_with_deflation = 0` on two substitution events. Zero events is not a measurement until you
ask what shape the event would have to have. E281 had already noticed that every stranded tail
publishes a **degenerate** multiplier range (`min == max == 1.0`), so this card turned that into a
quantity.

**The branch is a single point in multiplier space.** Reachability is E272's published contract
(`flip` inside the tail's published range), and a degenerate range `[v, v]` reduces the whole test to
`flip == v` at the published tolerance. Both stranded readings here sit at `v = 1.0` while their
flips are **2.7046** and **3.2544** -- the flip would have to be `2.70x` / `3.25x` smaller, or the
degenerate value that much larger, before the branch could fire.

**Turn the distance into the tolerance it would take.** Each candidate publishes
`tau_r = gap_pct_r / 100` (E272's own percent ruler, sign-free), so the branch becomes reachable
exactly when the tolerance is loosened to `tau* = min_r tau_r = 63.03 pct`, i.e. the band
`[63.03 pct, +inf)`. At the published tolerance (`1e-12` pct = multiplier equality to ~1e-14) it is
`False`, published as measured, not asserted.

**Then apply the loosened test to the whole family, because that is what loosening means.** At
`tau*` the *same* rule calls **21 of 24** published tail readings reachable (published: **2 of 24**,
87.5 pct of the face). So the tolerance that fires the branch is not a tolerance, it is a different
instrument: it declares almost everything reachable, which is exactly the state the family's
findings exist to distinguish rows from. That is the reusable point -- a "reachability threshold"
is only a threshold while the population still splits; publish the split at the threshold you are
proposing, not only the number.

Companion reading (same face, unasked): the *word* "inert" in the family is a claim about the
published multipliers, not about the tight tail's real behaviour -- the tail is inert because no
arm published a multiplier below 1.0, which E272 already disclosed. This card does not revise it.

Evidence: `scripts/e283_degenerate_range_reachable.py` (selftest 16/16, run/verify green),
`results/state_tilt/BANDDEFLATE-2026-10-29.json`, S6 leg `degenerate_range_reachable` (verify,
<1s), smoke leg `product: a contradiction branch that needs a 63 pct tolerance is not a test`,
digest `research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1308-e283-degenerate-range.md`. Pool item
`E283-DEGENERATE-RANGE-REACHABLE` (card ids drift from pool ids: pool E283 -> card E286).
Next card `E285-INTERRANGE-GAP-CEILING` (pool).
### E287 - a field that names one unit while publishing another (scope slip)
A summary field is all most readers see, so a field whose NAME promises rows while its VALUE is a
list of group labels over-claims coverage by the cells per group (4x in the case measured) and prints
identically to the correct reading. Repair = publish cell-scoped keys alongside, re-derived from the
face's own census (never re-typed from the summary), keep the old field as a group-scope bound, and
MEASURE the bound direction: group scope bounds cell scope from above only when no group holds a
second matching cell. Sweep the family mechanically by name vocabulary (group/leg/arm/family vs row)
-- 30 faces, 1 hit -- and disclose the integer count fields the sweep could not judge (1338) instead
of calling them clean. The identity partner is what makes the repair believable: the derived cells
must land exactly on the keys the face already published elsewhere (here its swap rows).
Evidence: `scripts/e284_disagreement_field_scope.py` (selftest 23/23, run/verify green),

### E288 - unreachable is not one thing: the gap between two ranges and the zone beyond the ceiling
Two published tails with different ranges leave a space BETWEEN them, and a reading that lands there
is reachable by neither -- but so is every reading beyond the widest published ceiling, and only the
first of those is widening headroom. Measure the classes as an exclusive partition
(reachable_tight -> reachable_wide -> in_gap -> above_ceiling -> below_floor) and assert the counts
sum to the rows censused, so no reading can be counted twice or quietly dropped. Price the gap in
each tail's own spread (the family's only ruler) and publish null where the ruler does not exist (a
degenerate tail has spread 0). Case measured (12 rows, 4 arms): 2 in a positive gap (20 pct of the
10 unresolvable), 6 above the published ceiling of 2.2963 (up to 1.417x it), 2 below the floor --
so any widening inside the published evidence can add at most the 2 gap rows while the extrapolation
zone is three times larger, and the two must never be summed into one "unreachable" number. The
identity that makes the counts believable: the class totals re-derive the source face's own
reachable counts (2 wide / 0 tight) and every gap row is published unreachable by both tails.
Evidence: `scripts/e285_interrange_gap_ceiling.py` (selftest 23/23, run/verify green),
`results/state_tilt/BANDGAPCEILING-2026-10-29.json`, S6 leg `interrange_gap_ceiling` (verify,
0.17s), smoke leg `product: the inter-range gap is a smaller widening target than the area beyond
the published ceiling`, digest `research/digests/DIGEST-20261031-r1310-e288-gap-ceiling.md`.
